analysis.one_liner: Bars health care discrimination and lets patients sue providers over unequal treatment.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate health committee in March 2024 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for health care providers to give patients worse care based on race, national origin, sex, disability, age, or religion. It would require hospitals to report patient outcomes broken down by demographics, let patients file complaints and sue for damages, allow the government to kick providers with a pattern of unequal care out of Medicare and Medicaid, add equity measures to hospital Medicare scoring, and create a standing Federal Health Equity Commission. It would also send grants to hospitals for bias training, translation services, and diverse hiring.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who receive lower-quality care because of who they are — the bill's findings cite evidence that Black patients and other minorities get worse care even with the same insurance and condition. Patients would gain a complaint process, the right to sue for actual and punitive damages, and new federal enforcement.

how_it_helps.text: Creates an enforceable right against inequitable health care, with complaints to a renamed Office for Civil Rights and Health Equity, investigations, conciliation, and private lawsuits carrying actual and punitive damages.

Requires hospitals and providers to report health outcomes disaggregated by race, national origin, sex, disability, and age, and builds a federal repository of that data to expose patterns of unequal care.

Adds equitable-care measures to the hospital Value-Based Purchasing Program, which ties a portion of Medicare payments to quality, and makes a pattern of inequitable care grounds for excluding a provider from Medicare and Medicaid — with an exception so exclusions don't reduce access in underserved communities.
Authorizes grants to hospitals for bias training, translation and interpretation services, diverse workforce recruitment, and outcome tracking, prioritizing hospitals serving low-income communities.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals and health care providers bear new reporting requirements, exposure to investigations and lawsuits, possible exclusion from Medicare and Medicaid, and changes to how Medicare pays them; taxpayers fund the new commission, data repository, and hospital grants.

drawbacks.text: The private right of action allows punitive damages and attorney's fees, which providers and their lobbyists warn invites costly lawsuits and defensive medicine; critics of similar bills argue courts would struggle to apply the 'high-quality care standard' to individual clinical decisions.

The bill tries to blunt this by requiring investigators to account for social determinants of health so providers are not held responsible for outcomes outside their control, and by barring exclusions that would make care harder to reach in underserved areas — but the 'inequitable provision of health care' definition remains broad and partly untested.
The bill authorizes spending 'such sums as may be necessary' for the commission and grants without identifying offsets, adding to federal health spending.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The enforcement model borrows directly from civil rights law in housing and employment, where private lawsuits and government enforcement are the established way to change behavior, so the design is not novel. The real trade-off is between giving patients a genuine remedy for unequal treatment and the litigation and compliance burden on hospitals, including safety-net hospitals that serve the very communities the bill aims to protect — the grants are meant to offset this, but only help providers that win them.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Alex Padilla introduced the bill in the Senate on March 22, 2024, with Sen. Cory Booker, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill never reached the Senate floor before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
The bill attracted only one cosponsor in the Senate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals and health care providers are better off, having avoided new civil rights liability, demographic reporting requirements, Medicare payment changes, and possible exclusion from federal health programs. Patients seeking enforceable protections against unequal care gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Alex Padilla
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill — the bill's only cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on March 22, 2024 and took no further action before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill's only support was two Democratic senators and it drew no Republican cosponsors.

industries.note: Hospitals would face equity measures in their Medicare value-based scoring, demographic outcome reporting, investigations and possible exclusion from Medicare/Medicaid, and private lawsuits — but would also compete for new federal grants for bias training and translation services. The industry's interest in avoiding enforcement and liability runs against the bill's goal of giving patients a remedy for unequal care.

industries.industry: Physicians and other health care providers
industries.note: Providers would face a new prohibition on inequitable care with a private right of action, punitive damages, attorney's fee exposure, and administrative investigations, though the bill excludes providers from punishment when poor outcomes stem from social factors outside their control.
